questions.text:
The box-and-whisker plots below compare the prices of two brands of running shoes from an NZ sports retailer website. Brand A has n = 80 shoes and Brand B has n = 95 shoes.

Approximately what percentage of Brand B running shoes cost more than $240?
questions.markingGuide:
From the box plot, Brand B upper quartile is $240.

By definition, 25% of values lie above the upper quartile.

So approximately 25% of Brand B shoes cost more than $240.

That is about 0.25 × 95 ≈ 24 shoes.

Award Achieved for 25% with reference to the upper quartile.

graph.title: Running Shoe Prices — Brand A vs Brand B

questions.text: Compare the distributions of the price of Brand A and Brand B running shoes. Discuss similarities and differences considering centre, shift, shape, and spread. Provide numerical evidence. What conclusion can you make about which brand is more expensive?
questions.expectedAnswer: Brand B is more expensive — median $185 vs Brand A median $90
questions.markingGuide:
Step 1: Centre: Brand B median ($185) much higher than Brand A ($90).

Step 2: Shift: Brand A UQ ($130) < Brand B LQ ($140), meaning no overlap in IQRs.

Step 3: Spread: Brand B has larger range ($530 vs $420) and larger IQR ($100 vs $70).

Step 4: Shape: Both right-skewed (long upper whisker).

Step 5: Conclusion: No IQR overlap strongly supports Brand B being more expensive.

Step 6: Achieved = one feature.

Step 7: Merit = two features.

Step 8: Excellence = comprehensive comparison with numerical evidence.

Final answer: Brand B is more expensive — median $185 vs Brand A median $90.

questions.text: Give at least one justified reason why the running shoe price data may not be reliable for comparing the two brands.
questions.expectedAnswer: Data from only one website, may not represent all retailers
questions.markingGuide:
Valid reasons: Data from only one website.

Unknown whether prices are sale or RRP.

Sample sizes differ (80 vs 95).

Only NZ prices — doesn't represent other countries.

Award Achieved for one justified reason.

questions.text:
The time series graph below shows quarterly NZ spending on sportswear from 2012 to 2024.

What trends, repeating patterns, and unusual features do you notice? Support with evidence from the graph. Give at least two reasons.
questions.expectedAnswer: Increasing trend ($500M to $750M), seasonal peaks in Q4 (Christmas)
questions.markingGuide:
Step 1: Trend: Long-term upward from ~$500M (2012) to ~$750M (2024).

Step 2: Repeating: Q4 peaks (Christmas).

Step 3: Unusual: COVID dip in 2020, supply chain spike in 2021.

Step 4: Achieved = one feature.

Step 5: Merit = two features with evidence.

Final answer: Increasing trend ($500M to $750M), seasonal peaks in Q4 (Christmas).

questions.text: Using the time series data on NZ sportswear spending (2012-2024), make a prediction about future spending. Explain your prediction and discuss how confident you are.
questions.expectedAnswer: Spending will continue to rise, following long-term upward trend
questions.markingGuide:
Step 1: Prediction: Likely to continue increasing.

Step 2: Seasonal Q4 peaks will persist.

Step 3: Confidence: Reasonable for 1-2 years as trend is established.

Step 4: Less confident long-term due to economic changes, technology shifts.

Step 5: Achieved = prediction with basic reasoning.

Step 6: Merit = prediction with justified confidence discussion.

Final answer: Spending will continue to rise, following long-term upward trend.

questions.text:
The scatter plot below shows the relationship between cushioning level (1-10) and price ($) for 25 pairs of running shoes.

Describe and interpret TWO different features of the relationship shown in the scatter plot.
questions.expectedAnswer: Positive trend — shoes with higher cushioning cost more. Two clusters: budget (levels 3-5) and premium (levels 7-10)
questions.markingGuide:
Features: Positive relationship (higher cushioning = more expensive).

Two apparent clusters (budget levels 3-5, premium levels 7-10).

Wide price variation at each cushioning level.

Award Achieved for two features.

graph.title: Running Shoe Price vs Cushioning Level

questions.text: Tama wants running shoes with a cushioning level of 8. Using the scatter plot, what price should he expect to pay? How confident can you be in this prediction?
questions.expectedAnswer: About $1000-$1250 from the scatter plot. Moderate confidence — there is reasonable data at level 8 but prices range from $900 to $1250
questions.markingGuide:
Step 1: Reading from scatter plot: approximately $1000-$1250 for cushioning level 8.

Step 2: Confidence: Moderate — level 8 has 3 data points ranging from $900 to $1250, showing some spread.

Step 3: Achieved = reasonable price reading.

Step 4: Merit = price AND justified confidence.

Final answer: About $1000-$1250 from the scatter plot. Moderate confidence — there is reasonable data at level 8 but prices range from $900 to $1250.

questions.text:
Three retailers sell the same running shoe model. The table below shows their pricing.

GST rate is 15%. Ricky wants one pair of shoes. Which retailer should he choose? Show all calculations.
questions.expectedAnswer: Factory Outlet (collecting) at $943 is cheapest. SportZone: $1107.50. Shoe World (No GST deal): $1008.
questions.markingGuide:
Step 1: SportZone: $950 × 1.15 = $1092.50 + $15 delivery = $1107.50 (no free delivery because it is below $1200).

Step 2: Shoe World with No GST deal: $1150 ÷ 1.15 = $1000 + $8 delivery = $1008.

Step 3: (With 5% loyalty instead: $1150 × 0.95 + $8 = $1100.50.) Factory Outlet collecting: $820 × 1.15 = $943.

Step 4: With delivery: $820 × 1.15 + $25 = $968.

Step 5: Cheapest overall = Factory Outlet collecting at $943.

Step 6: Achieved = one correct calculation.

Step 7: Merit = two correct retailer totals.

Step 8: Excellence = comprehensive comparison of all three with correct conclusion.

Final answer: Factory Outlet (collecting) at $943 is cheapest. SportZone: $1107.50. Shoe World (No GST deal): $1008..

questions.text: Ricky currently has running shoes with cushioning level 5 but wants to upgrade to a higher cushioning level. Using the scatter plot data and the retailer pricing, recommend the best purchasing option for Ricky.
questions.expectedAnswer: Consider Factory Outlet for best base price, but factor in travel costs to warehouse if not collecting
questions.markingGuide:
Step 1: Key points: Higher cushioning shoes cost more (scatter plot shows level 7-10 range $800-$1800).

Step 2: Factory Outlet has lowest base price but requires collection.

Step 3: If Ricky lives far from warehouse, delivery cost matters.

Step 4: Shoe World with loyalty card may be better if he already has one.

Step 5: Achieved = one relevant point.

Step 6: Merit = points from multiple sources.

Final answer: Consider Factory Outlet for best base price, but factor in travel costs to warehouse if not collecting.

questions.text:
A survey of 2400 NZ adults asked about their exercise habits. 48% said they exercise at least 3 times per week.

Approximately how many of the 2400 respondents exercise at least 3 times per week?

The pie chart below shows the preferred exercise types from the survey of 2400 NZ adults.

Which exercise is the most preferred? Discuss how confident you would be in concluding this is genuinely the most popular.
questions.expectedAnswer: Running 24%, but Gym (21%) and Swimming (18%) close — not highly confident
questions.markingGuide:
Step 1: Running is most preferred at 24%.

Step 2: However, Gym (21%) is very close.

Step 3: Range across top three is only 6 percentage points.

Step 4: Large sample (2400) helps but small differences mean a different sample could change rankings.

Step 5: Achieved = identifies Running.

Step 6: Merit = discusses confidence.

Final answer: Running 24%, but Gym (21%) and Swimming (18%) close — not highly confident.

questions.text:
The table below shows the most popular exercise type for different age groups.

Discuss two similarities or differences in exercise preference by age. Suggest what exercise Mia (age 34) might prefer.
questions.expectedAnswer: Younger prefer running, older prefer lower-impact. Mia likely running or gym.
questions.markingGuide:
Step 1: Differences: Younger people prefer running, older prefer lower-impact activities (swimming, walking).

Step 2: In the 25-35 bracket, running and gym are tied.

Step 3: For Mia (34): in the 25-35 bracket, either running or gym.

Step 4: Achieved = one comparison.

Step 5: Merit = two comparisons AND recommendation.

Final answer: Younger prefer running, older prefer lower-impact. Mia likely running or gym..

graph.title: Most Popular Exercise by Age Group

questions.text: James is 50, exercises 4 times per week, mostly swimming. Using survey data (by age group and frequency), recommend an exercise type and estimate how much he might spend on it monthly. Include evidence from at least two data sections.
questions.expectedAnswer: Swimming — most popular for 46-55 age group. Budget $80-$120/month based on pool pass data.
questions.markingGuide:
Step 1: James is 46-55 where swimming is most popular.

Step 2: He already swims 4× per week.

Step 3: Survey shows 52% of exercisers spend $50-$150/month.

Step 4: Recommendation: Continue swimming, budget $80-$120/month for pool membership.

Step 5: Achieved = recommendation with one piece of evidence.

Step 6: Excellence = comprehensive with cost estimate.

Final answer: Swimming — most popular for 46-55 age group. Budget $80-$120/month based on pool pass data..

questions.text: How confident would you be using information from this survey to make recommendations about exercise habits?
questions.expectedAnswer: Moderately confident — large sample (2400) but may not represent all NZ adults
questions.markingGuide:
Step 1: Strengths: Large sample (2400).

Step 2: Detailed breakdowns by age and frequency.

Step 3: Weaknesses: Unknown how respondents were selected.

Step 4: Self-reported data (people may overestimate exercise).

Step 5: May not include all demographics equally.

Step 6: Achieved = one strength or weakness.

Step 7: Merit = both discussed.

Final answer: Moderately confident — large sample (2400) but may not represent all NZ adults.
